action_criteria.rationale: A year of magnetic gait with urge incontinence and an outside report of enlarged ventricles needs an MRI that measures the ventricles and excludes an obstruction before any CSF is removed.

action_criteria.label: Lumbar tap test with opening pressure and CSF removal
action_criteria.rationale: Normal-pressure CSF and an objective response to removing 30 to 50 mL support probable iNPH and predict shunt benefit in this patient with incomplete DESH.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the syndrome to normal ageing or deconditioning once the ventriculomegaly and the tap response are documented
Do not restart oxybutynin or another anticholinergic bladder drug for the urge incontinence, as oxybutynin already worsened his cognition
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 25% in TUG at 24 hours, the supportive MRI (Evans index 0.31, acute callosal angle, enlarged temporal horns) and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

Counsel that gait is the symptom most likely to improve after shunting, and that the benefit for memory and for the urinary symptoms, which may partly reflect benign prostatic hyperplasia, is less predictable

avoided_actions.rationale: He has no episodes suggesting seizures, so an EEG cannot help separate iNPH from its mimics.
His falls are mechanical, with no syncope or palpitations, so an ECG does not inform the gait work-up.
There is no syncope, murmur or embolic event, so echocardiography has no role in this work-up.
An MRI is available and measures the callosal angle, temporal horns and aqueduct better than CT.
The falls are not syncopal, so rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role here.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are
Normal-pressure CSF with a normal cell count in a chronic afebrile gait syndrome gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious assays.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Fazekas grade 2 white matter change can add to gait and executive slowing, but ventricles enlarged out of proportion to it, an acute callosal angle and a 25% TUG improvement after the tap make iNPH the main cause.
Mild leg tone increase without rest tremor, upper-limb rigidity or bradykinesia, preserved postural reflexes and a gait that improved after CSF removal argue against parkinsonism.

His father had Alzheimer's disease and free recall is reduced, but recall improves with cues, the hippocampi are MTA 1 and the gait disorder came first, which does not suggest Alzheimer's disease as the main cause.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventricles out of proportion to the sulci, an acute callosal angle, temporal horns larger than the hippocampal volume explains and a tap response argue against atrophy ex vacuo.
There is no history of head trauma, subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis or intracranial surgery.

key_clinical_evidence: Insidious gait disturbance over one year from age 67 with urge incontinence and mild cognitive slowing, and no antecedent trauma, haemorrhage or meningitis, meets the clinical criteria for probable iNPH; the full triad is not required [Relkin_2005]

MRI shows Evans index 0.31 with an acute callosal angle (82 degrees), temporal horns enlarged out of proportion to the hippocampi and a patent aqueduct; DESH is incomplete (tight convexity sulci, Sylvian fissures not enlarged), so the supportive features are the callosal angle and the temporal horns [Relkin_2005] [Nakajima_2021]

Opening pressure 16 cmH2O with normal CSF content; after 40 mL was removed, TUG improved 25% at 24 hours (22 to 16.5 s) and the 10-metre walk 21%, above the commonly used 10% TUG criterion [Nakajima_2021]

Tap-test sensitivity is 26% to 61% with a PPV of 73% to 100%, so a positive tap supports shunting while a negative one would not have excluded it; extended lumbar drainage is more sensitive [Marmarou_2005]
Fazekas grade 2 white matter change makes a vascular contribution likely but does not preclude a shunt response [Tisell_2011]
Urge incontinence despite tamsulosin is probably mixed (iNPH-related detrusor overactivity and benign prostatic hyperplasia); oxybutynin was stopped because it worsened his cognition
Reduced toe vibration and ankle reflexes of 1+ may reflect age or a mild diabetic neuropathy, which adds sensory unsteadiness but does not produce a magnetic gait that improves after CSF removal

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The mildly reduced toe vibration and ankle reflexes of 1+ may reflect age or a mild diabetic neuropathy, which can add unsteadiness but does not cause a short-stepped magnetic gait with start hesitation that improves after CSF removal.
red_herrings.data_point: Type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin, with reduced toe vibration and ankle reflexes of 1+
red_herrings.intended_effect: Gait ataxia is attributed to diabetic peripheral neuropathy

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]

patient.history_present_illness: A 68-year-old right-handed retired civil engineer with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and benign prostatic hyperplasia was admitted for evaluation of progressive gait difficulty, urinary incontinence and memory decline. The patient reports approximately one year of progressive gait deterioration which has significantly affected his quality of life. His wife describes his gait as having become 'shuffling and unstable' — he takes small steps, rarely lifts his feet off the ground, and has had three falls in the past six months, including one that resulted in a bruised right elbow. He requires furniture or wall support to turn around. He has stopped walking outside unassisted and has not driven in four months after his wife expressed concern about unsafe driving. Concurrently, over approximately the same period, he has developed increasing difficulty with urinary urgency and incontinence. He has had five episodes of urinary incontinence in the past three months despite taking tamsulosin for BPH. His urologist has attributed the urinary incontinence to worsening BPH and added oxybutynin (which was subsequently stopped due to cognitive side effects). On questioning, his wife reports he is somewhat more forgetful than one year ago, primarily forgetting appointments and recently repeating questions, but he remains able to manage finances and plan. A brain MRI obtained 6 weeks ago at an outside facility was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available. His primary care physician referred him for neurological evaluation, and after an outpatient neurology visit he was admitted for further assessment.

neurological_exam.additional: No cogwheel rigidity. No resting tremor. No postural instability on pull test (does not fall backward).
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact. Heel-shin mildly impaired on left.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive, 3mm bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Tongue midline. Hearing intact to finger rub bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Short-stepped, shuffling, broad-based gait (magnetic gait). Step height markedly reduced; feet barely clear the floor. Start hesitation with freezing at gait initiation. Slow cadence. Takes several steps to turn. Tandem gait impossible.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, attentive and fully oriented, with slowed responses. Speech fluent and coherent. No aphasia, apraxia, or agnosia. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk. Mild bilateral lower extremity tone increase (difficult to distinguish from rigidity vs passive resistance). Upper extremity tone normal. Strength 5/5 throughout. No tremor.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ biceps, triceps, brachioradialis bilaterally. Patellar 2+ bilaterally. Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Vibration reduced at toes bilaterally (age-appropriate). Light touch intact.
